question: Each of the \(9\) squares in a \(3 \times 3\) grid is to be colored red, blue, or yellow in such a way that each red square shares an edge with at least one blue square, each blue square shares an edge with at least one yellow square, and each yellow square shares an edge with at least one red square. Colorings that can be obtained from one another by rotations and/or reflections are to be considered the same. How many different colorings are possible?
solution:
Starting from the center, the neighbor requirements force a chain of colors. Rotations and reflections let us place that chain in a standard position.

First count colorings whose center is red, and write \(R,B,Y\) for the three colors. The center needs a blue neighbor. Rotate the grid to place one on its right. That blue square needs a yellow neighbor, which must be one of the two right corners. Reflect across the horizontal middle line if necessary to make the top right corner yellow.

That yellow corner needs a red neighbor, forcing the top middle square to be red. The top middle red square needs a blue neighbor, forcing the top left corner to be blue. This blue corner then needs the middle left square to be yellow. The grid now has the form
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
B&R&Y\\
Y&R&B\\
a&t&b
\end{array}.
\]
Only the bottom row remains. Its possibilities are summarized below.

| Bottom middle \(t\) | Bottom left \(a\) | Bottom right \(b\) | Number |
|---|---|---|---:|
| \(B\) | Impossible | Impossible | 0 |
| \(Y\) | \(B\) | \(R\) or \(B\) | 2 |
| \(R\) | \(B\) | \(R\) or \(Y\) | 2 |

To justify the table, if \(t=B\), it needs a yellow corner beside it. Either such corner would have no red neighbor, so this case fails.

If \(t=Y\), the bottom left corner has two yellow neighbors, making blue its only possible color. The bottom right corner has blue and yellow neighbors, so it can be red or blue. Both choices work.

If \(t=R\), the bottom right corner cannot be blue because neither of its neighbors is yellow. Thus the bottom middle red square must obtain its blue neighbor from \(a\). With \(a=B\), either \(b=R\) or \(b=Y\) gives a valid coloring.

We have found four standard representatives, but must check that none are equivalent. In all four, the right middle square is the only blue neighbor of the center. Any symmetry between two representatives must therefore keep that position fixed. Only the identity and horizontal reflection can do so.

For three representatives, the bottom right corner is not yellow, so horizontal reflection would fail to leave a yellow top right corner. The remaining representative has bottom row \(BRY\), identical to its top row, so that reflection fixes it. Therefore the four representatives give four distinct classes.

Cyclically relabeling \(R\to B\to Y\to R\) preserves the rules, so each center color gives four classes. Spatial symmetries preserve the center color, keeping these three collections distinct. The total is
\[
3\cdot4=\boxed{12},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{C}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
We can first distinguish the grid's top, bottom, left, and right, then group these oriented colorings into symmetry classes. Colorings with reflection symmetry need separate treatment because they have fewer distinct orientations.

Begin with a red center, and call its four edge-sharing neighbors the side squares. Choose a blue side square, which must exist. It needs a yellow corner beside it. That yellow corner forces its other neighboring side square to be red. This red side square needs a blue neighbor, forcing its other corner to be blue. That blue corner forces the next side square to be yellow, opposite the blue side square we started with.

Thus every blue side square has a yellow side square opposite it. We have also forced a red side square next to the original blue one. The fourth side square cannot be blue, since its opposite is red. There is therefore exactly one blue side square.

There are four choices for its position. For the moment, place it on the right. The left side square is yellow. The top and bottom side squares must include a red square and cannot be blue, leaving these cases:

| Top side square | Bottom side square | Corner fillings |
|---|---|---:|
| Red | Red | 3 |
| Red | Yellow | 2 |
| Yellow | Red | 2 |

In the first case, both left corners must be blue to supply the top and bottom red squares with blue neighbors. Each right corner can be red or yellow, and the blue right side square needs at least one yellow corner. The ordered right-corner pairs are therefore \((Y,R),(R,Y),(Y,Y)\), giving three fillings.

In the second case, the top left corner must be blue to serve the top red square. The bottom left corner lies between two yellow squares, so it must also be blue. The bottom right corner cannot be yellow because it would lack a red neighbor. Consequently, the top right corner must be yellow to serve the blue right side square. The bottom right corner can be red or blue, giving two fillings. Reflecting these arrangements exchanges the second and third cases, so the third also gives two.

Every filling described satisfies all the rules. Since the unique blue side square identifies its position, these cases do not overlap. There are
\[
4(3+2+2)=28
\]
oriented colorings with a red center. Cyclic relabeling of the colors gives \(3\cdot28=84\) oriented colorings in total.

Now identify the symmetric ones. The unique side square of the color required by the center rules out every nonidentity rotation. It also forces any reflection axis to pass through that square and the center.

With a red center and the blue side square on the right, the only possible axis is horizontal. The top and bottom side squares must then both be red. Among their three corner fillings, only the one with both right corners yellow is symmetric. Thus there is one symmetric coloring for each of four blue-side positions and each of three center colors, totaling \(12\).

The four rotations of every coloring are distinct. A coloring with a reflection symmetry has only these four orientations; otherwise reflection supplies four additional orientations. Hence the number of symmetry classes is
\[
\frac{12}{4}+\frac{84-12}{8}
=3+9=\boxed{12},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
